items.originalTitle: ‘Grandfather’ or ‘godfather’? Republicans know they’re stuck with Trump
items.author: Andrew Howard and Aaron Pellish
items.title: ‘Grandfather’ or ‘godfather’? Republicans know they’re stuck with Trump
items.summary: Republican leaders grappling with how to recover after their devastating midterm losses agree on one thing: President Donald Trump isn't going anywhere in 2028, even if some wish he would. Interviews with more than two dozen GOP state and county officials from red, blue and purple states across the country conducted since Election Day revealed a party still processing their election drubbing and at a loss for how to move forward. Some want to move on from Trump entirely. Some are eager for his involvement. And others are just resigned that he’s going to do whatever he wants, regardless of their preferences. All of them are worried about the party’s chances of retaining control of the White House in two short years, but they also recognize its current occupant is going to continue to exercise a huge role in the future of the party. “President Trump is going to be part of it, whether we want that or not,” said Arkansas GOP chair Joseph Wood. “His voters are still going to be Republicans that we need to have come out in this election in two years.” That leaves the party in a precarious position. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found the president’s approval rating at 32% overall, and at 70% among Republicans — down from 91% on inauguration day last year. A POLITICO Poll taken after the midterms found 56% of Trump’s 2024 voters believe the Republican Party needs to distance itself from him and his agenda. But no one in the party expects that to happen. And Trump has already taken steps to maintain his grip on the GOP, endorsing Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters for another term and ordering his powerful super PAC to continue fundraising ahead of 2028. A handful of Republican grassroots leaders were openly critical of Trump. “I don't know how much he really has to offer,” said Vermont GOP chair Paul Dame. “I think most people are ready to move on in a new direction.” Added Michael Bub, the chair of ruby-red Taylor County, Wisconsin, Republican Party :“He should stay out of it. Look at the people he endorsed: They lost.” In a statement, RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassare said “President Trump remains the unequivocal leader of our party.” “Republicans will continue to harness his ability to energize our voters and expose the Democrats' disastrous record to win in 2028,” she said. The White House demurred, pointing to the RNC’s response. Many party officials are resigned to Trump doing whatever he wants, given his domineering personality and strong sway over the party base. Nebraska Republican Party Chair Mary Jane Truemper said “Donald Trump's going to play whatever role he wants to play.” “He's the president,” Truemper said. “I look at things as they are and not as I want them to be.” That’s leaving some state-level Republican leaders wanting the president to take on a more constructive role and be willing to let other candidates and ideas rise. “I hope he becomes kind of the mentor grandfather, and not the godfather,” said Kansas GOP chair Danedri Herbert. “In America, we hope and expect our presidents to not keep a tight grip on the party, to recognize that now it's time for me to mentor the next generation.” Added outgoing Minnesota Republican Party Chair Alex Plechash: “We need to capitalize on what he brought to the party and do what we can to retain that. But there has been a definite turn in the political landscape.” Virtually every GOP official cited the poor political environment caused in part by the president’s handling of the economy and the war in Iran as the reason for the party’s midterm meltdown. But many stopped short of laying the blame directly at the president’s feet, a sign of how criticism of Trump is still verboten within the party. “I don't want to play the blame game, because I just don't think it's productive,” said West Virginia GOP chair Josh Holstein. “But I do think that it was more economics than it was anything.” Many GOP chairs praised the president’s ability to bring in new voters to the party and credited him for working to turn those voters out on behalf of other candidates. Still, some said they hope Trump’s generation-defining tenure at the top of the party comes to an end, allowing Republicans to choose the nominee without his influence. “Republicans should embrace whoever we decide we're going to get behind as a new president, and let the Trump era be gone by the time we're in 2028,” said Oklahoma GOP chair Charity Linch. Ben Proto, Connecticut’s GOP chair, said he is focused on what he and the RNC can control ahead of 2028 — and wants to make sure the organization stays neutral. “We shouldn't put our hand on the scale,” he said of the 2028 primaries. “I think Republican primary voters are pretty savvy and pretty smart and can figure out who our best candidate is going into the ’28 election.” Trump still has plenty of defenders. Even some chairs who are bucking Trump’s endorsement of Gruters and backing RNC co-chair KC Crosbie’s challenge to him, like Kentucky chair Robert Benvenuti, think Trump should continue to be heavily involved in 2028. “He won't take a back seat and should not take a back seat,” Benvenuti said. “I think he's been a tremendous leader for our country. … I think his message will still ring true and will be very helpful as we go into 2028.” Samuel Benson, Lauren Fedor and Jason Beeferman contributed to this report.

items.author: Andy Tomaswick
items.title: Fermi's 14-year all-sky map bridges astronomy's elusive 'MeV gap'
items.summary: Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot. We've always had trouble measuring them in the "megaelectronvolt" (MeV) energy range, which astronomers have taken to calling the "MeV gap." But a new paper from an international group of scientists working with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) Collaboration, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series, takes a stab at closing that gap by identifying 450 cosmic sources in the 20–200 MeV range, providing the clearest view of low-energy gamma rays ever.

items.originalTitle: Ebola’s Death Toll Tops 5,700. Can the Outbreak Be Contained?
items.author: Rebecca Schneid
items.title: Ebola’s Death Toll Tops 5,700. Can the Outbreak Be Contained?
items.summary: Kenya Red Cross personnel in personal protective equipment simulate the evacuation of remains of an Ebola victim in the Kenyan capital Nairobi on Oct.22, 2026. —Tony Karumba—AFP via Getty Images The Ebola outbreak that originated in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has surpassed 11,700 confirmed cases and 5,700 deaths as of Nov. 19 , making it the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country’s history and the second-deadliest worldwide. Katie Thomas-Canfield, who is based in Bunia, Congo, and serves as the Ebola response director for the International Rescue Committee, tells TIME that this outbreak’s deadly pace is informed by numerous converging factors. “There's some element of it that is a perfect storm, and there's some very specific elements of this moment in time that have contributed to the fast evolution,” Thomas-Canfield says. The latest outbreak crossed the 10,000-case mark in just 163 days—51 days sooner than the West Africa epidemic in 2014-2016, which was the world’s deadliest Ebola outbreak. It shows no signs of slowing as cases spread beyond Congo. Beyond Congo, Uganda has reported 20 confirmed cases and two deaths, Kenya nine cases and two deaths, and Nigeria one case. France confirmed a case in June in a doctor returning from a humanitarian aid mission in Congo. In November, a British doctor who tested positive in Congo was flown to London for treatment and has since recovered. Read more: Ebola Returns: How We Can Fight Back Thomas-Canfield and other experts argue that delayed detection, the specific strain of the virus being spread, and mistrust within the affected communities toward health care providers are all hampering the response—and suggest what needs to happen next. Delayed detection Experts tell TIME that there are several reasons why this outbreak has spread so quickly and resisted containment. A main contributor was late detection, according to Dr. Abdou Sebushishe, a senior health adviser with the nonprofit International Medical Corps. There was a large gap between when the outbreak started and when it was discovered, he says. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), it’s estimated that the outbreak began in mid- to late-February, two to three months before the outbreak was detected and declared an emergency by the World Health Organization (WHO) in mid-May. “It’s quite serious because we now don't have access to all the [contacts] of the first case,” Sebushishe says. “All those people have moved a lot in different locations, and with limited access, not all the [contacts] can be reached, and that is one of the factors, as well, that has contributed to this outbreak to be bigger.” Experts have linked this gap in surveillance to humanitarian cuts from countries around the globe in 2025. For example, the Trump Administration dismantled the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) in 2025, which led to cascading impacts on humanitarian and development efforts abroad. During the 2014 West Africa epidemic, USAID was the lead federal agency coordinating the international U.S. government response. But Thomas-Canfield says that the stripping of humanitarian aid has not stopped with USAID cuts. “There were the cuts in the U.K ., the cuts in Germany , the cuts elsewhere, and that has collectively undermined our global capacity to both surveil [and] identify potential new biomedical hazards that are emerging—and to respond early enough to be able to actually prevent their scale,” she says. Many countries, in the face of the current outbreak’s severity, have increased their funding to combat the crisis—something Thomas-Canfield says is helpful, but does not change the fact that there were not enough health care workers to stop the pandemic before it grew in those initial months. “We saw that partners were not present to the same extent that they used to be present in these areas, and a lot of the risk-education community relationships that are required did not happen, and there was no long-term presence and visibility in communities,” she says. “Equally, you also saw an erosion of the community surveillance work that historically has been really important in raising alarms early and promptly.” A difficult strain of the virus and frequent population movement Containing the spread has been especially challenging because the outbreak is driven by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, a rare variant for which no approved vaccines or targeted antiviral treatments exist—though vaccine trials are currently being developed . The Bundibugyo strain causes different symptoms that aren’t always immediately recognized as Ebola. It doesn’t tend to cause the “wet” symptoms that people associate with past outbreaks of the more common Zaire strain—including bleeding from orifices, vomiting, and diarrhea. This means that Bundibugyo is frequently confused with other common tropical illnesses—such as malaria—in the earliest stages of infection. “What we're seeing is a longer period of these dry symptoms that are very innocuous that do resemble very closely some of the diseases that are most endemic to this area, straight to mortality,” Thomas-Canfield says. “So a lot of the telltale signs that bring people to clinics in time to be able to receive treatment aren't there in quite the same case numbers, fueling misinformation.” With high population movement across the country—due to regional conflict and urbanization—and without adequate surveillance in place to catch these symptoms quickly, health care workers are chasing a moving target of hotspots across the country. Thomas-Canfield says that her team has seen the number of health zones that were impacted jump from 60 to at least 68 since Sept. 1. When she spoke to TIME in early November, she shared that she had just heard a rumor about a case in a new health zone. “As soon as we're getting it under control in one area, there are new areas that are cropping up,” she says, “and because of how long it takes us to establish the relationships for communities to trust us, that means we're already behind in the response.” Health officials work at the One-Stop Border Post in Busia, Kenya, Oct. 16, 2026. —John Okoyo—Xinhua via Getty Images Struggles in building trust Distrust of health care workers is a persistent issue in containing the outbreak. In the summer, that distrust fueled violence against medical workers , with reports of violent mobs attacking burial workers and response teams. Within the first six months of the outbreak, there were a reported 260 attacks on health workers, according to the U.N. Those attacks have continued into the fall. “Community resistance is not new,” says Sebushishe. When information is hard to share as fast as the disease spreads, he says, “it creates a lot of rumors around the isolation, around the response itself.” As TIME previously reported , poor communication about care in isolation units left some families believing their loved ones were being separated unnecessarily. Resistance also arose when safe burial protocols conflicted with mourning traditions, such as washing and preparing the bodies of loved ones. Sebushishe adds that communities also are often distrustful when they see disparities in the humanitarian response to Ebola compared to their everyday medical aid. “People say: ‘We have been dying with malaria for so long, and there is no support that we've received,’” he says. This pushback to healthcare can be dangerous for workers and contribute to escalating spread. “Resistence of community causes more people to die at home or in private health facilities or informal care, and there they contribute the spread of the disease because there are no enough containment measures in place,” Sebushishe says. The attacks themselves can also contribute to the spread of disease, as patients who witness the attacks may flee back to their communities while they are still contagious. What needs to change Experts tell TIME that there are actions countries can take to get the outbreak under control. One is to ensure clinics have the equipment and training necessary to combat localized cases. Because patients may not immediately suspect that they have Ebola, the vast majority are first seen by primary and secondary health care clinics, Sebushishe says. These clinics have very limited capacity to address the outbreak. Reinforcing these front-line clinics, strengthening their surveillance capacity, and enabling access to personal protective equipment and other preventative measures will help to lower transmission rates, he says. “Then a lot of cases can be picked from primary health care level and be referred or isolated on time—that will cut the transmission from going further,” Sebushishe explains. He adds that the kinds of community-engagement measures that were implemented in Ituri—where the outbreak began in Congo and where the vast majority of cumulative confirmed cases remain—need to be implemented across the country. “Community-based surveillance and a lot of information to be provided door by door to the community needs to happen—not only in Ituri, not only in North Kivu, but in high-risk locations where population movement is frequent between those affected areas and the non-affected areas,” he says. This community engagement is essential, according to Thomas-Canfield, to ensure that health care workers get “buy in” from citizens, and make sure response teams are able to assuage fears from the community and have meaningful engagement. Thomas-Canfield adds that another factor must change in order for containment to occur: global border response. “In 2014, we saw that, broadly, borders remained open with the U.S. They remained open with Europe, and that again facilitated first responders and technical expertise from the CDC, in particular, traveling to West Africa,” she recalls. Given how “novel” the virus is, she says there are not many experts in its containment, and the ability for those with the knowledge to access and work with local experts is paramount. She notes that borders have shuttered across North America and in a handful of other nations in 2026. Humanitarian and aid workers from the United States, for example, are permitted to travel to Congo, but returning is more complicated. Potential travelers must show that they have been out of Congo for at least 21 days before they are permitted to enter the United States. “It's a massive disadvantage,” she says, pointing to the WHO’s advice against border closures during Ebola outbreaks. Rather than stop movement, border closings redirect movement into informal routes with no health screenings, making it even harder for health care officials to trace outbreaks, according to the WHO. “Closure of borders is not an effective mechanism to prevent the spread of Ebola. That is not science-based,” Thomas-Canfield says. While opening borders could help with disease management, what’s needed most is the development and dissemination of a vaccine that works against the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola. The University of Oxford is developing one, and it is currently undergoing clinical testing. Early results have been encouraging, but whether it can prevent disease—and when it could become widely available—remains uncertain. At the same time, there is a trial underway to learn if the Ervebo vaccine, which was approved for the Zaire strain, would have any impact on Bundibugyo. “Vaccines are a huge draw for hope in the response,” Thomas-Canfield says, while acknowledging that “trial finalization, evidence, and confirmation of efficacy are still some time out.” Even when a vaccine becomes available, health workers will need to engender community support in order to ensure people will accept them. Thomas-Canfield says that there are already rumors circulating in Bunia with vaccine misinformation. Like all other public health measures, she says vaccines can “only be as effective as the strength of our community relationships and trust.”

items.title: New Democratic governors race to deliver relief on costs
items.summary: PARK CITY, Utah — Cost-of-living concerns fueled Democrats to victory this month. Now they’re preparing to do something about it. As newly elected governors gathered for a job training conference hosted by the National Governors Association, conversations among the Democrat-heavy group often turned to the economic woes in their states — and the necessity to get something done quickly. “What are the things that we can do — not in the first 100 days, but in the first 100 hours — that can start bringing some relief to the American people?” Wes Moore, the National Governors Association chair and Maryland governor, said in an interview with POLITICO. Health care and home costs topped the target list. Several newly elected Democratic governors — Jocelyn Benson in Michigan, Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, Deb Haaland in New Mexico and Rob Sand in Iowa — plan to take action to lower health costs, ranging from caps on prescription drug prices to expanding Medicaid coverage, within days of taking office. California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra promised to spur affordable housing construction. His Nevada counterpart, Aaron Ford, said he plans to limit corporations purchasing private homes, and is preparing a day-one executive order to task every state agency with “finding ways to put money back in people's pockets.” “You hear people signing executive orders to make things easier for businesses, cut regulations, and make it easier to do business. I think that's cool, that's fine, that's dandy,” Ford said in an interview. “But if you can do it for businesses, you can do it for people, too.” Affordability was, far and away, the top issue for voters this cycle. Results from The POLITICO Poll, conducted just days after the midterm elections, found a 47% plurality of Americans — including 59% of Democratic voters and 41% of Republicans — said affordability and the economy were among the main issues driving their vote. Democrats’ tsunami washed over governors’ mansions across the nation: They won 24 of the 36 governor’s races held this month, flipping red states like Texas, Alaska and Ohio, and will hold 30 of the 50 governorships nationwide next year — the most in three decades. These governors and soon-to-be governors will be buoyed by a boon of Democrats in their statehouses: Democrats won unified control of government in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada and Wisconsin; in North Carolina, Democrats flipped the House for the first time in 16 years and broke Republicans’ supermajority in the Senate. As several inches of snow descended on the Wasatch Front and blanketed the glitzy ski resort in Park City this week, the newly elected governors sheltered inside the NGA’s New Governors Leadership Forum — colloquially called “baby governors’ school.” At the two-day seminar, the incoming state executives and their teams attended seminars and workshops, mingled over hors d'oeuvres and heard from current and former governors on what to expect. Former President Bill Clinton, sitting spread-legged in a Team USA sweater Thursday, dished to a room full of governors on his book recommendations (“The Social Conquest of Earth” by E.O. Wilson), fun facts (“The combined weight of ants on earth exceeds the combined weight of all the people on earth!”) and political predictions (“I think if President Trump gets closer to leaving, he may get more interested in leaving actual legacies in forms other than buildings.”) Clinton, who chaired the NGA when he served as governor of Arkansas, also offered some advice to the newly electeds: “The most important thing is that you and your Cabinet and your office and your organizations out in the state know what your priorities are and know what your progress is.” Governors will face a steep climb to deliver immediate relief to Americans. Economic forces are national and international, and much of the past year’s price spikes, from fuel to food to energy, can be tied to the Iran war. Bottoms said she will immediately begin to prepare Georgia agencies for Medicaid expansion, and expects the state legislature — with Democrats now in control of the state House, while Republicans still control the state Senate — to cooperate. “I do believe this is an issue we will get bipartisan support on,” she told POLITICO. In addition to his Day-One executive order, Ford says he plans to work with the Nevada legislature to sign bills in his first 30 days on expanding free public school meals, lowering the cost of prescription drugs to the Medicaid negotiated price and limiting corporations’ ability to buy private homes. Benson said she has already reached out to the Trump administration about tariffs, which includes a 50% tariff on most Canadian exports and have disproportionately impacted Michiganders. She said she has not yet heard back, but “the point is I have reached out, and I do hope to have that conversation.” She also emphasized her focus on lowering health care costs. “That's life or death for so many families,” Benson said. Megan Messerly and Adam Wren contributed reporting.

items.originalTitle: A Robbie Williams film starring a CGI chimp helped me come to terms with my hearing loss
items.author: Dr Robert Mote
items.title: A Robbie Williams film starring a CGI chimp helped me come to terms with my hearing loss
items.summary: I was bullied for my deafness as a child, and just when I was finding myself, a car crash set me back years. But then I watched the movie Better Man, and had my life explained for me I cannot say I’ve ever been a Robbie Williams fan. When I went to see Better Man, the 2024 biopic in which Williams is played by a CGI chimp, I was tagging along with my wife. To be honest, I was sceptical about the ape but tried to meet the film with an open mind. I wasn’t looking for anything in particular but what I found was something that seemed to explain my life. I was born two months premature in Winnipeg, Canada, in 1961, with severe hearing loss in both ears that wasn’t diagnosed until I was seven. In 1969 we moved to Woking in Surrey; my father left and my mother descended into alcoholism. I was a misfit in my family, with no support for my deafness, and at school the bullying – from kids and teachers – was something awful. In my desperate isolation, I turned to reading: book reading, lip-reading, and reading the room. Forget TV, forget music – the Beano andBeezer were my survival manuals: the Numskulls taught me how my brain worked with broken ears.

items.title: Teenager cooking meals for family after mother's death now has 2 million social media followers
items.summary: 18-year-old Joey Charney's mother died of breast cancer in August, so he started cooking meals for his family and documenting his dishes on social media. Now he has over 2 million followers. Steve Hartman goes on the road.

items.originalTitle: ‘People couldn’t deal with watching an animal die’: the strange saga of Timmy the whale – and how a whole country lost its mind
items.author: Ben Knight
items.title: ‘People couldn’t deal with watching an animal die’: the strange saga of Timmy the whale – and how a whole country lost its mind
items.summary: When the humpback got stranded on Germany’s Baltic coast, crowds gathered, conspiracy theorists pitted themselves against scientists and animal lovers argued with vets. Why did the animal trigger such an intense derangement? What surprised Bodo Köpnick was how loud the whale was. “You could hear it as far away as the next village. It was eerie, but also impressive,” he says, then pauses to think how best to describe the noise a suffering humpback makes at night. “It was like a cow moaning. It went to your marrow.” Köpnick, 65, is everything you would hope for in a volunteer fire chief on a sleepy holiday island: a grandfatherly figure who mostly spends his weekends teaching local children about health and safety, and letting them climb on the engines. But on 31 March his life was made infinitely more stressful by the appearance of a lost whale that had got itself stranded on the shores of his island of Poel, in northern Germany. It became his fate to stand on the shoreline and guard the huge creature while behind him an entire country lost its mind.

items.originalTitle: Federal court indefinitely pauses military's plans for detonation of unstable explosives in Iowa
items.title: Federal court indefinitely pauses military's plans for detonation of unstable explosives in Iowa
items.summary: The Army's plan to detonate five tons of unstable bomb-making material containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa was put on indefinite hold by a federal court Friday amid environmental and health concerns. Lana Zak reports.

items.originalTitle: Race to lead Senate Democrats the latest battlefield in party’s tussle over Israel
items.author: Alice Speri
items.title: Race to lead Senate Democrats the latest battlefield in party’s tussle over Israel
items.summary: Chris Van Hollen and Chuck Schumer represent conflicting visions on issue that has become ‘litmus test’ for Democratic voters The race to lead the Democratic Party’s incoming Senate majority has become the latest battlefield between two conflicting visions for how the US should relate to Israel – a once unquestioned ally whose collapsing standing among the US public has become a defining feature of American politics. Chuck Schumer, the veteran New York Senator and current Democratic minority leader, is one of Israel’s most reliable supporters in Congress. As he views it, according to an interview he gave last year, his “job” is to “keep the left pro-Israel”.
